query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a small amount of oxygen or nitrogen interstitials into a refractory high-entropy alloy can improve its high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloy in its as-cast or wrought state
generation.intervention: Introduction of a small amount of oxygen or nitrogen interstitials
generation.conditions: High-temperature mechanical testing, such as tensile or compressive testing, at temperatures above 500°C
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of ordered interstitial complexes (OOCs/ONCs) that impede dislocation motion and enhance strain hardening
generation.mechanism: Solid-solution strengthening and the formation of ordered interstitial complexes (OOCs/ONCs) that impede dislocation motion and enhance strain hardening, derived from materials-science principles
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature mechanical capability, such as increased yield strength and elongation, while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance
generation.boundary: Temperature range of 500°C to 1000°C, strain rates of 10^-3 s^-1 to 10^-1 s^-1
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of oxygen or nitrogen interstitials required, the optimal composition of the refractory high-entropy alloy, and the potential effects of other alloying elements

falsification_experiment.design: High-temperature mechanical testing of refractory high-entropy alloys with and without oxygen or nitrogen interstitials
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of oxygen or nitrogen interstitials does not result in improved high-temperature mechanical capability, the hypothesis is falsified

System: Quaternary W-Ta-V-Cr high-entropy alloy with atomic composition 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V. Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Question: How can the compressive strength of the NbMoCrTiAl refractory high-entropy alloy be improved for high-temperature structural applications while maintaining oxidation resistance?. System: NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy matrix with in-situ formed TiC and Al2O3 reinforcement particles.
